title: The Nuniyya of al-Busti
intro: The Nuniyya, “the poem rhyming in nun”, also called Unwan al-Hikam, “the heading of wise sayings”, is Abu al-Fath al-Busti's best-known poem: the editors of his diwan call it “among the best-known poetry of his age”, and the only long poem by a man whose pieces rarely reached twenty lines. It has no love prelude and no patron: it opens by declaring that whatever a man gains in this world is loss, promises sayings set out “as rubies and coral are set”, and then gives one in almost every line, on kindness, forgiveness, the fear of God, gentleness, contentment, friends and counsel, before warning the young man and the greybeard and handing the whole over as “proverbs made to travel”. It is full of the wordplay al-Busti was famous for: “whoever is generous with his mal, wealth, people mala, lean, towards him”. The proverbs did travel: his friend al-Tha'alibi recast most of its lines as prose maxims, Ibn al-Qayyim quoted its “servant of the body”, al-Suja'i and Nuqrakar wrote commentaries on it, and the modern scholar Abd al-Muhsin al-Qasim, who says Nuniyya is the better-known name, includes it among the set texts students learn by heart.

translation: Whatever a man gains of this world is a loss,
and his profit, if it is not purely good, is ruin.
1.sharh: Every increase in worldly goods is really a decrease, since a man must answer for it and it draws him from the next life; any profit not made in pure good is a loss. Each half pairs opposites: increase and decrease, profit and loss.

translation: Every piece of luck that is found and does not last
is, when you look into it truly, a loss.
2.sharh: Anything a man comes by that will not stay with him is, rightly seen, already lost, because it is bound to vanish. Wijdan, finding, and fiqdan, losing, share one pattern and sound while meaning opposite things.

translation: You who toil to build up a house that is bound for ruin,
by God, can a ruined life ever be rebuilt?
3.sharh: He asks the man who labours over a house that will fall in the end whether a life, once wasted, can be built again: a house can be repaired, spent years cannot. The line plays on one root: amir, builder, umr, lifetime, and umran, rebuilding.

translation: And you who are greedy for wealth, gathering it,
have you been made to forget that the joy of money is sorrow?
4.sharh: He turns to the man who hoards money: the pleasure it gives becomes grief, in the labour of keeping it, in leaving it at death, and in answering for it. The question is a rebuke, not a request for information.

translation: Restrain your heart from the world and its finery:
its clear water is muddy, its union is parting.
5.sharh: The heart should be held back from the world, whose pleasures are never clear of trouble and whose embrace is already a farewell. Each blessing is paired with its opposite: clear and muddy, union and separation.

translation: Lend me your ear for sayings I will string apart,
as rubies and coral are strung apart.
6.sharh: He asks for attention and promises a string of sayings, set out like the stones of a necklace in which rubies alternate with coral. From here on almost every line is a separate maxim, a gem in its own setting.

translation: Be good to people and you will make their hearts your slaves;
kindness has often enslaved a man.
7.sharh: Kindness wins hearts so completely that the one who receives it becomes, as it were, the giver's slave. Insan, man, and ihsan, kindness, differ by a single letter. The modern commentator al-Qasim objects to “enslave” and would rather read “win over”.

translation: And if someone does wrong, let there be in you,
whenever his lapse comes to light, pardon and forgiveness.
8.sharh: When someone does harm, each lapse should be met, as it appears, by overlooking and forgiving it rather than by taking him to task. It extends the kindness of the line before to those who have not earned it.

translation: Servant of the body, how you toil to serve it.
Do you look for profit where there is only loss?
9.sharh: He addresses the man who spends himself caring for his body and its appetites: the body will perish, so all that labour is an investment that can only lose. The next line names what deserves the care.

translation: Turn to the soul and perfect its virtues:
you are human by the soul, not by the body.
10.sharh: The soul deserves the care, and its virtues should be brought to completion, for it is the soul, not the flesh, that makes a man human; the body he shares with the beasts. A hadith in Muslim says that God looks at hearts and deeds, not at faces and wealth.

translation: Be, against the blows of fortune, a ready helper to the man with hopes
who looks to your generosity: the free man is ever ready to help.
11.sharh: A man should stand by whoever hopes for his generosity and help him through the hardships fortune brings, since helping others is the mark of the noble. Mi'wan is an intensive form: not one who helps once, but one who helps again and again. Al-Tha'alibi's prose version: “the free man is a helper against time”.

translation: Hold fast with both hands to the rope of God,
for that is the pillar when other pillars fail you.
12.sharh: God and His religion are a support that stands when every other prop, wealth, rank or friends, gives way. The rope echoes the Quran: “hold fast, all of you, to the rope of God” (3:103).

translation: Whoever fears God is praised in the outcome of his affairs,
and is spared the harm of the mighty and the lowly.
13.sharh: The affairs of a God-fearing man end well, and God protects him from everyone's malice, strong or weak. The Quran says “the outcome belongs to piety” (20:132); the mighty and the lowly together stand for all people.

translation: Whoever seeks help from other than God in any pursuit,
his helpers are weakness and abandonment.
14.sharh: Whoever relies on anyone but God for what he needs will be helped only by failure and desertion, that is, not at all. Calling weakness and abandonment his “helpers” is a bitter irony.

translation: Whoever keeps good from others
has, in truth, no brothers and no close friends.
15.sharh: A man known for withholding help, whether money or influence, has no real friends, however many hang around him. Ikhwan, brothers, and akhdan, intimates, differ by a single letter.

translation: Whoever is generous with his wealth, all people lean towards him;
wealth is a temptress to mankind.
16.sharh: Generosity draws everyone, for money seduces both those who hope for it and those who own it. The line turns on two words spelled and said alike: mal, wealth, and mala, leaned.

translation: Whoever keeps the peace with people is safe from their treachery,
and lives content and glad.
17.sharh: The man who leaves people in peace is left in peace: he escapes their plots and lives untroubled and happy. Salama, to make peace, and yaslam, to be safe, come from one root, so the reward echoes the deed.

translation: Whoever lets reason rule over him
becomes a man over whom greed has no rule.
18.sharh: A man who puts his mind in charge of himself breaks the hold of greed, since reason checks appetite. Both halves end on sultan, “power”: given to reason, denied to greed.

translation: Whoever, in the excess of his ignorance, lets his eyes stray to desire
will one day lower them before the truth, in shame.
19.sharh: The man who out of folly lets his gaze reach for what he craves will one day have to drop his eyes, ashamed, before the truth. The eyes that stretch out at the start close at the end; al-Qasim takes “the Truth” as God.

translation: Whoever lives among people meets weariness from them,
for wrong and aggression are their very grain.
20.sharh: Living among people is tiring, because injustice is in their nature. That is no reason to withdraw: a hadith in Ahmad's Musnad prefers the believer who mixes with people and bears their harm to the one who does neither.

translation: Whoever pries into his friends will come to loathe them:
most brothers of this age are traitors.
21.sharh: Digging into friends' secrets only breeds dislike, since most friends nowadays are false; better to take people as they seem. Ikhwan, brothers, already contains the letters of khawwan, traitor.

translation: Whoever consults the turns of fortune
is given proof of fortune's true nature.
22.sharh: Ask time's changes for advice and they show plainly what time is: nothing in it stays. Time is made an adviser who, when consulted, testifies against himself.

translation: Whoever sows evil reaps, in the end,
regret; and the reaping of a crop has its season.
23.sharh: Evil is a seed whose crop is remorse, and that crop will be gathered when its time comes, however late. The whole line is one farming image: sowing, reaping, and the season for reaping.

translation: Whoever rests his trust in the wicked has gone to sleep
with a viper and a serpent from them inside his shirt.
24.sharh: Trusting bad men is sleeping with snakes in one's clothes: sooner or later they strike. Istanama, to rest one's trust in, and nama, slept, share a root, so the trust and the fatal sleep are one act.

translation: Wear the freshness of a cheerful face: a noble man's spirit
is a letter, and cheerfulness is the address written on it.
25.sharh: A noble spirit is like a folded letter, and a cheerful face is the address on the outside: the first thing people read, and the sign of what lies within.

translation: Keep gentleness as your companion in everything:
no gentle man has ever regretted it, and no one has blamed him.
26.sharh: Gentleness should go with a man in all he does; no one gentle has ever had cause to regret it or been reproached for it. Rafiq means both “gentle” and “companion”, so the gentle man is gentleness's companion.

translation: Do not be fooled by luck that rashness brought:
rashness pulls down, and a man's gentleness builds.
27.sharh: A fool's hasty success should tempt no one; recklessness wrecks in the end what it seemed to win, while patient gentleness builds what lasts. Pulling down and building complete the praise of gentleness in the line before.

translation: Do good while you have the means and the power:
the means to do good never last.
28.sharh: Generosity should not wait: wealth and office pass, and the chance to do good passes with them. Imkan, “the means”, appears in the first half and comes back as the rhyme.

translation: As a garden is adorned with its blossoms in full scent,
the free man is adorned with merit and kindness.
29.sharh: Kindness is to a noble man what flowers are to a garden: the thing that makes him beautiful. The verb yazdan, “is adorned”, appears in both halves, setting the garden and the man side by side.

translation: Guard the free of your face; do not tear its veil:
every free man is a careful keeper of his face's honour.
30.sharh: Dignity should be kept intact, not thrown away by begging or anything shameful, as one might rip a fine undergarment. Hurr means both a free, noble man and the best part of a face, and the line uses both.

translation: And if you meet an enemy, always meet him
with your face fresh with cheer and brightness.
31.sharh: Even an enemy should always meet a bright, cheerful face, never a scowl: a smile blunts hostility and gives him nothing to work on. Al-Tha'alibi's prose version of the line reads: “put out the fire of enmity with the water of cheerfulness”.

translation: Give up sloth in going after good deeds:
no idler is made happy by good deeds.
32.sharh: Good works reward only those who hurry to them; the lazy never taste their joy. The Quran says “race one another to good deeds” (2:148); sloth opens the line and the sluggard closes it.

translation: A man stripped of piety and sense has no shade,
though leaves and branches shelter him.
33.sharh: Without the fear of God and good sense a man is exposed, however leafy the trees over his head; the only real shelter is piety. The Quran calls it a garment: “the garment of piety, that is best” (7:26).

translation: People are the helpers of the man whose turn of fortune favours him,
and when it turns against him they are helpers against him.
34.sharh: People side with whoever is in luck, and the same people side against him the moment his luck turns. The word “helpers” opens and closes the line, first for him, then against him.

translation: Sahban without money is Baqil, tongue-tied,
and Baqil, rich in money, is Sahban.
35.sharh: An eloquent man who is poor passes for a stammering fool, and a stammering fool who is rich passes for an orator: money decides who is eloquent. The two proverbial names simply swap places.

translation: Do not entrust a secret to a talebearer who cannot hold it:
no wolf ever shepherded sheep in the open desert.
36.sharh: Telling a secret to a gossip is like leaving sheep in a wolf's care in the wilderness: he will devour it. Sirr, secret, is echoed in sirhan, wolf.

translation: Do not think people are all of one nature:
they have temperaments beyond counting, and many colours.
37.sharh: People differ endlessly in character, noble and mean, loyal and false, so each should be treated according to what he is. A hadith in Muslim says that people are like mines of silver and gold.

translation: Not every water is like Sadda' to the one who comes to drink,
yes, and not every plant is sa'dan.
38.sharh: Not all water is as sweet as the famous well of Sadda', nor all pasture as rich as sa'dan; people are not all alike either. The line packs in two proverbs: “water, but not like Sadda'” and “pasture, but not like sa'dan”.

translation: Do not scratch the face of a kindness with delay:
a good deed is scarred by putting off and stalling.
39.sharh: A favour delayed is a favour spoiled: putting off what was promised mars it, as a scratch mars a lovely face, even if it is delivered in the end.

translation: Seek counsel only from a man who is able, resolute and alert,
in whom private and public are the same.
40.sharh: Advice should be sought only from someone capable, firm and wide awake, and sincere through and through, who will not say one thing while thinking another.

translation: Planning has its horsemen who, when they gallop into it,
outstrip all others, as war has its horsemen.
41.sharh: Good counsel has its champions as battle does; when they gallop into a problem they leave everyone behind, and they are the ones to consult. Horsemen appear in both halves, the second ending on them.

translation: Affairs have their appointed times,
and everything has its limit and its measure.
42.sharh: Everything comes at the time set for it and within its proper bounds, so there is no use forcing it early. The line prepares the warning against haste that follows.

translation: So do not be hasty over the thing you seek:
a crisis is not welcome before the illness has ripened.
43.sharh: Nothing should be rushed. Physicians of the time held that a fever must “ripen” before its crisis, the sudden turn towards recovery or death; a crisis that came too early was a bad sign, and so is success snatched too soon.

translation: Enough of living is whatever has met your need:
in that a free man has both possessions and wealth.
44.sharh: What covers a man's needs is enough; for a free man it is all the property and all the riches he requires. Qunyan, possessions, and ghunyan, sufficiency, differ only in their first letter.

translation: The contented man is pleased with his livelihood,
and the greedy man, even when he grows rich, is angry.
45.sharh: Contentment makes a little enough, while greed is never satisfied: the greedy man resents his lot however rich he becomes. Contentment and greed, pleasure and anger, face each other.

translation: A young man's mind is friend enough to keep him company
when brothers and companions keep away.
46.sharh: When friends desert him, a man still has his reason, a companion that never leaves and always gives good advice. Khill, friend, comes back in the plural khullan, companions.

translation: Two who were suckled together: wisdom and piety;
two who share one home: wealth and tyranny.
47.sharh: Wisdom and the fear of God are foster brothers who never part, and riches and arrogance live under one roof. The Quran says that man transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient (96:6–7).

translation: If a homeland grows hostile to a noble man,
beyond it, across the wide earth, he has homelands.
48.sharh: A noble man need not stay where he is unwelcome: the earth is broad and holds many homes. Mawtin, homeland, returns in the plural awtan at the rhyme.

translation: You wrongdoer, glad of the power that has favoured you,
you may be dozing, but time is wide awake.
49.sharh: The oppressor who revels in his good fortune may be heedless, but time is watching and will repay him. Drowsiness and wakefulness are set face to face.

translation: Injustice never agreed with the one who devours it, if you are fair:
does bitter colocynth ever please a man's taste?
50.sharh: Looked at honestly, no oppressor really enjoys what he has seized, just as no one relishes colocynth, the bitterest of gourds. Injustice is made a food, and the food a poison.

translation: You scholar whose conduct is approved,
rejoice: you are quenched without water.
51.sharh: The learned man who lives well has a source of refreshment that needs no water: knowledge satisfies the soul as water does the body. The next line turns the image round.

translation: And you, brother of ignorance, though you were amid the deep seas,
there among them you would surely be thirsty.
52.sharh: The ignorant man could stand in the middle of the ocean and still be parched, because what he lacks no water can supply. It mirrors the line before: the scholar is quenched without water, the fool thirsty in a sea of it.

translation: Do not think any happiness lasts for ever:
whomever one time has pleased, many times have grieved.
53.sharh: No joy is permanent: one happy season is paid for with many unhappy ones. The pleasing time is singular, zaman, and the grieving times plural, azman.

translation: If a friend you were close to grows cold to you,
look for another: all people are brothers.
54.sharh: No one should cling to a friend who has turned away; another can be found, for brotherhood is open among all people. Al-Qasim limits “people” to believers, citing “the believers are brothers” (Quran 49:10).

translation: And if the lands where you grew up turn against you,
move on: all God's lands are homelands.
55.sharh: When his native country will not let him live well, a man should leave it; every land belongs to God and can become a home. It restates line 48, again ending on awtan, homelands.

translation: You who swagger in lush youth, giddy
from its cup: has a drunken man ever found the right way?
56.sharh: Youth intoxicates like wine, and a drunk man never finds his way; the young man strutting in his prime should know that his elation clouds his judgement. Al-Tha'alibi's prose version: “the drunkenness of youth is the drunkenness of wine”. The reciter's rahl, “saddle”, makes no sense here, so the translation follows the editions' wahf, “lush”.

translation: Do not be deceived by youth that is bright and fresh:
how many young men have gone ahead of the grey-haired.
57.sharh: Youth is no promise of a long life; many young men die before the old, or, as al-Tha'alibi put it, an old man may carry a child's coffin. Shabab, youth, shubban, young men, and shib, the grey-haired, sound alike while pointing to opposite ends of life.

translation: And you, brother of grey hair, if you were honest with yourself,
one like you would not plunge on into excess.
58.sharh: Turning from the young man to the old, he says grey hair is a warning: a man near his end who gave himself honest advice would not go on squandering his life in sin.

translation: Grant that youth may offer an excuse for the young;
what excuse has a grey-haired man whom the Devil leads astray?
59.sharh: Youth, with its heat and recklessness, may excuse a young man's sins, but an old man whose passions have cooled has no excuse. A hadith in Muslim names the old adulterer among those God will not speak to on the Day of Judgement.

translation: Every sin, God forgives it,
if sincerity and faith go along with a man.
60.sharh: No sin is beyond God's forgiveness for one who turns back to Him sincerely and in faith. It answers line 58 with the Quran: “you who have been excessive against yourselves, do not despair of God's mercy” (39:53).

translation: Every break, religion can mend it,
but for a break in the shaft of religion there is no mending.
61.sharh: Faith consoles every worldly loss, but when faith itself is broken nothing can set it. Religion is pictured as a spear, the thing a man leans on and fights with; snap its shaft and he has nothing left.

translation: Take them, proverbs made to travel, polished:
in them, for whoever seeks clarity, is clarity.
62.sharh: He hands over the poem as polished sayings meant to circulate, offering plain guidance to anyone who wants it. The word for clarity, tibyan, comes back as the rhyme: whoever seeks clarity finds clarity.

translation: What harm to their Hassan, his nature being their goldsmith,
if Hassan, the champion of poets, did not fashion them?
63.sharh: The poet makes light of his work: it does him no harm that these sayings, shaped by his own gift, were not made by Hassan ibn Thabit, the Prophet's poet. He calls himself “their Hassan”, and the goldsmith recalls the rubies and coral of line 6.

3.1.4.head: الدّار
3.1.4.meaning: The house. The diwan and al-Qasim have al-dahr, “time”; the reciter follows Abu Ghudda, the margin of the diwan's manuscript and al-Tha'alibi.

3.2.5.meaning: Umran: building up, restoration; from the same root as umr, lifetime.

6.1.4.head: فَصَّلَ
6.1.4.meaning: I will string them apart, as in a necklace where a bead separates each pair of pearls.

6.2.4.head: مَرجان
6.2.4.meaning: Marjan: coral; some commentators took it for small pearls.

8.2.1.meaning: Urud: appearing; here, whenever his lapse shows itself.

11.1.4.head: مِعوان
11.1.4.meaning: Mi'wan: one who helps much and often.

12.1.3-4.meaning: “The rope of God”: His religion and His Book, from Quran 3:103. The diwan has “the rope of religion”.

16.1.4.meaning: Leaned, inclined; it looks and sounds like mal, wealth, just before it.

17.2.3-4.meaning: “Cool of eye”: content, at peace; tears of joy were thought cool and tears of grief hot.

20.2.2.head: سوس
20.2.2.meaning: Sus: the stock or grain of a thing, its inborn nature.

21.2.4.head: العَصر
21.2.4.meaning: Age, era. Al-Qasim's text has al-dahr, “time”; the reciter follows the diwan, Abu Ghudda and al-Tha'alibi.

24.2.3.meaning: Sill: a snake with a deadly bite.

25.2.4.meaning: Unwan: the address or heading written on the outside of a letter. The poem's other name, Unwan al-Hikam, uses the same word.

26.2.2.meaning: Rafiq: gentle; the same word means a companion.

27.1.5.meaning: Kharaq: clumsy rashness, the opposite of gentleness.

29.1.3.head: الأَنوار
29.1.3.meaning: Anwar: blossoms, plural of nawr, a flower; the same letters spell “lights”.

30.1.2-3.meaning: “The free of your face”: its noblest part, the face's honour.

34.1.5.head: دَولَة
34.1.5.meaning: Dawla: a turn of fortune, luck that passes from one man to another; the word also means a dynasty or state, and al-Qasim takes it as the ruler's favour.

35.1.1.meaning: Sahban Wa'il: an orator proverbial for eloquence, “more eloquent than Sahban Wa'il”.

35.1.5.meaning: Baqil: a man of Iyad proverbial for being tongue-tied; asked what he had paid for a gazelle, eleven dirhams, he held up his ten fingers and stuck out his tongue, and the gazelle got away.

36.1.6.head: مَذِل
36.1.6.meaning: Madhil: one who cannot hold a secret. The diwan and Abu Ghudda have “a talebearer who gives it away”.

38.1.4.head: صَدّاء
38.1.4.meaning: Sadda': a well whose water was proverbially the sweetest.

38.2.6.meaning: Sa'dan: a thorny plant, the best of camel pasture.

39.1.5.meaning: Arifa: a kindness, a favour done.

39.2.4.head: لَيّان
39.2.4.meaning: Layyan: stalling over a debt or a promise.

40.1.4.meaning: Nadb: quick and capable in getting things done.

43.2.5.meaning: Buhran: the crisis of a fever, a physicians' term.

44.2.3.meaning: Qunyan: what one acquires and keeps.

47.1.2-3.meaning: “Two sucklings of one milk”: foster brothers, an idiom for two things that always go together.

48.1.2.meaning: Was unkind to, would not let him settle; literally “shied away from”.

49.2.4.meaning: Sina: drowsiness, the first touch of sleep.

50.2.5.meaning: Khutban: colocynth when it is streaked green and at its most bitter.

52.1.2-3.meaning: “Brother of ignorance”: one who is never without it.

56.1.5.meaning: Rahl, as the reciter clearly says it, means a saddle or a traveller's baggage and does not fit; the diwan, al-Qasim and al-Tha'alibi have wahf, “thick, lush” (of hair or plants), and Abu Ghudda rahb, “ample”.

57.1.5.meaning: Fresh, blooming. Al-Qasim reads it so in his commentary; his printed text and the diwan have khadil, “moist, lush”.

57.2.4.head: الشّيب
57.2.4.meaning: Shib: men gone grey. The diwan reads shayb, “grey hair”: before grey hair comes.

62.1.2.meaning: Sawa'ir: sayings that travel, passing from mouth to mouth.

63.1.3.head: حَسّان
63.1.3.meaning: Hassan: here the poet himself, as the one who made them beautiful (husn), punning on the name of Hassan ibn Thabit.

63.2.6.meaning: Hassan ibn Thabit: the Prophet's poet, of the Ansar of Medina.
